V04.intro: The diagram separates the physical pathway from the paired recordings and the later calculation of predicted eye position.
V04.caption: The recordings pair one motor neuron with eye movement. Private spike variability acts at individual cells, downstream physical variability acts on movement, and measurement noise enters the eye-position record. The attractor storage source is proposed; the dashed analysis path is a calculation from one cell through its calibrated filter. Original guide schematic based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figs. 1–2 and 4–5. Signal symbols are illustrative, not experimental traces.
V04.alt: A proposed attractor storage circuit sends shared drive to a motor neuron population, then through muscles and eye mechanics to physical eye position. Private variability enters one neuron; downstream physical variability enters the muscles. Only the highlighted neuron is recorded, paired with eye position. Measurement noise enters that recorded position, not the physical eye. A separate dashed calculation transforms the single-cell spikes through a calibrated filter into predicted eye position.
V04.interpretation: The upper path describes a possible physical source and its output. The recording design provides one cell and eye movement at a time; it does not measure covariance between simultaneously recorded motor neurons. The predicted position is a later analysis result, not a signal sent backward through the physical pathway.

V05.intro: The calculated curves show how the same one-pole filter separates stationary white input from a wandering stored position.
V05.caption: Filtering stationary white input produces an MSD plateau; filtering Brownian stored position preserves long-lag growth. Each panel uses its own normalization, $M_{\mathrm{white}}/(A/\tau)$ and $M_{\mathrm{Brownian}}/(2D\tau)$, so the figure compares shapes without matching physical noise amplitudes. Original guide calculation for the one-pole teaching model, connected to Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Fig. 3 and main Eqs. 20–22; these are not measured data or the fitted full-model curves.
V05.alt: Two alternative inputs pass through identical one-pole filters. On matched logarithmic lag axes x equals lag divided by tau, normalized white-input MSD is 1 minus exp(-x), rising with short-lag slope one and approaching a plateau of one. Independently normalized filtered Brownian MSD is x minus one plus exp(-x), starting with slope two and continuing to grow with long-lag slope one. The two vertical scales differ.
V05.interpretation: The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example. The paper uses a smoother muscle response and additional motor filtering and feedback. The useful contrast is the plateau versus continued accumulation, not equality of the curves’ physical amplitudes.
